In the United Kingdom's 2024 general election, 650 members of Parliament were elected to the country's House of Commons – one for each parliamentary constituency.[1]

The UK Parliament consists of the elected House of Commons, the House of Lords, and the Sovereign.[2] The new Parliament first met on 9 July 2024.[3] Of the 650 MPs elected, more than half (335) were new to Parliament.[4]

House of Commons composition

[edit]

The Conservative Party under Prime Minister Rishi Sunak lost over 240 seats and its 14-year long tenure in government. The Labour Party formed a majority government under the leadership of Keir Starmer, winning over 400 seats. Other parties including the Liberal Democrats, Reform UK and the Green Party saw an increase in their seat share in the House of Commons at expense of the Conservatives and the Scottish National Party.

This table relates to the composition of the House of Commons after the 2024 United Kingdom general election. As of 8 July 2026[update], it summarises the changes in party affiliation that took place during the 2024–present Parliament.

Defections, suspensions and resignations

[edit]

The label under which MPs sit in the House of Commons can change if they leave or are suspended from or expelled by their party. When suspended, they effectively become independents.

  6. 1 2 3 Sinn Féin's seven MPs follow a policy of abstentionism. They do not swear into the House of Commons, and do not take part in its formal processes. As a result, they are not able to sit or vote in the House of Commons.[10]
